metadata.title: Reading more, achieving more? Long-term gender gaps in reading behavior and reading achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study constructs country-by-year gender gaps in reading achievement and free-time reading behavior by aggregating student questionnaire and test data across six PIRLS-related cycles (1970, 1991, 2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). For the achievement gender gaps, the authors explicitly state that they applied sampling weights and then combined results across five plausible values using Rubin’s (1987) rules. For the behavior gender gaps, they use student-reported questionnaire items and compute standardized gender-gap effect sizes at the country-by-year level; the paper does not specify a separate weight variable for the behavior component, but the overall approach is consistent with weighted aggregation. Replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not reported, so uncertainty quantification is described via PV combination rather than replicate-based variance estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that it excluded children with missing gender information and that one control variable (gender gap in early literacy activities) was missing for seven country-by-year observations, but it does not describe a formal missing-data handling method for the remaining variables (e.g., listwise deletion vs imputation) at the analytic stage. Because the study’s key outcomes are country-level gender-gap estimates derived from weighted student data and PVs, the missing-data strategy is only partially documented, representing a reporting gap rather than a clearly specified imputation/deletion protocol.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The unit of analysis is country-by-year observations constructed from six reading-comprehension assessment cycles (1970, 1991, 2001, 2006, 2011, 2016) linked onto a common achievement scale. The authors include only countries/regions that participated in at least two of the six cycles, yielding 212 country-by-year observations, and then exclude country-by-year observations where one third or more of students attended single-sex schools (operationalized as schools with at least 10 students in the RCS/RLS/PIRLS samples who were all boys or all girls). They also exclude children with missing gender information. Additionally, they run a reduced-sample robustness specification for models including control variables, restricting to countries participating in at least two PIRLS cycles (2001–2016), and the early literacy activities control is missing for seven country-by-year observations, reducing the sample size for that model.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS-linked reading comprehension (RCS 1970, RLS 1991, PIRLS 2001/2006/2011/2016) — end of primary school reading achievement (country-by-year gender gaps)
main_findings.target_variable: Gender gap in reading achievement (Cohen’s d units)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-fixed effects Model 2: b = 0.11 (SE = 0.05), p < .05 (two-tailed). Baseline Model 1: b = 0.08 (SE = 0.04), p < .05. Robustness Model 3 (PIRLS-only cycles): b = 0.12 (SE = 0.06), p < .05. Control models: Model 4 b = 0.12 (SE = 0.06); Model 5 b = 0.11 (SE = 0.06), one-tailed p < .05; Model 6 b = 0.10 (SE = 0.06), one-tailed p = .065. Multiple R²: 0.624–0.718 across models.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS-linked reading comprehension data (RCS 1970, RLS 1991, and PIRLS 2001/2006/2011/2016) to model country-by-year gender gaps in reading achievement, the study leveraged the gender gap in free-time reading behavior (and, in robustness models, controls for single-sex schooling, age, and early literacy activities) to predict the gender gap in reading achievement, finding that increases in the reading-behavior gender gap are associated with increases in the reading-achievement gender gap (Model 2: b = 0.11, p < .05). This indicates that policies aiming to narrow gender differences in boys’ and girls’ leisure reading may help reduce gender gaps in early reading achievement, though the fixed-effects design still cannot fully rule out time-varying confounding or reverse causality.

data.outcome_summary: This study links reading achievement and questionnaire-based reading behavior across six PIRLS-related cycles (1970–2016) to create a country-level longitudinal dataset of gender gaps at the end of primary school. The main outcome is the gender gap in reading achievement measured in Cohen’s d units on a common achievement scale, while the key predictor is the gender gap in free-time reading behavior (also in Cohen’s d units), computed from standardized questionnaire items across cycles. The authors estimate country-fixed effects regressions (unit: country-by-year; 192 observations after excluding high single-sex-school shares) and apply sampling weights and Rubin’s rules to combine results across five plausible values for achievement. The main model shows a positive association (b = 0.11, SE = 0.05, p < .05), with robustness across PIRLS-only cycles and models including time-varying controls, though the early-literacy control model loses statistical significance due to reduced sample size. Limitations include partial comparability of behavior items across early cycles, missing-data documentation for some controls, and causal interpretability constraints typical of fixed-effects observational designs.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an ML prediction/classification paper: it uses longitudinal country-fixed-effects regression to test associations between gender-gap trends, so ml_techniques are intentionally empty. The dataset is constructed from multiple ILSA cycles and aggregated to the country level, meaning there is no student-level ML model, no PV-based predictive algorithm, and no ML-specific performance metrics such as AUC or RMSE.
